text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse:
This is the song
That weaves together several of the songs
About one beautiful country-girl
Who was forcibly separated from her shepherd boy lover
And taken to Shlomo.1[1] It is with both excitement and apprehension that I present my interpretative and accessible translation of Shir HaShirim based on the commentary of the great 19th century Malbim – Rabbi Meir Leibush ben Yehiel Michel Wisser. In his commentary, Malbim brilliantly joins the dots and weaves together a seemingly disparate series of poetic dialogues and the occasional bit of narrative text into a coherent plot—a deeply moving romantic drama that progresses with palpable tension. The reader's allegiances are not immediately obvious as they embark on the rollercoaster of the tumultuous conflict faced by the country girl. However one precisely interprets the conflict—whether as the conflict between primal love and sensibility, between autonomy at all costs versus profitable conformity, or, as the Malbim himself interprets it, between spiritual yearnings and physical gravity—the plot is gripping, the language is artistic, and the text emotive. Following in the footsteps of the Sages who declared the work "the Holy of Holies," and aligning with the vast majority of Orthodox Jewish medieval commentators, Malbim unequivocally insists that this text is intended to be read metaphorically. While love, romantic passion, and physical beauty are often lauded throughout the Biblical texts—with patriarchs, matriarchs, and heroines deliberately described as beautiful people—the intensity of the language and imagery in the Song of Songs is, in my opinion – with the exception of a short excerpt in Proverbs – unparalleled in the Bible. It is almost overwhelming, bordering on the explicit. As Maimonides notes, the Hebrew tongue's accolade—Lashon Hakodesh, the holy tongue—is the result of its care and sensitivity when discussing potentially erotic content, with a highly constricted and at times euphemistic vocabulary subtly employed. Yet, within these “holy” confines, this “holy of holy” work loudly engages with the world of passion, romance and sensuality. This tension is well addressed in a fascinating Midrashic account regarding the copper used to construct the wash basin (Kiyor) in the Tabernacle. The Sages taught that it was crafted from the copper mirrors used by Jewish women to decorate themselves, arouse their husbands' romantic passions, and build their families even in the dire circumstances of Egyptian servitude. G-d and Moshe disagreed over whether it was appropriate for such mirrors to be reconstructed as a feature within Temple worship—where man communes with the Divine in a transcendent and spiritual manner. While Moshe's reaction was one of disgust, G-d's position ultimately prevailed, emphasizing how much He cherished those tools that create peace between a husband and wife. I suggest that there are echoes of this fundamental tension in how the religiously sensitive reader relates to Shir Hashirim. While there is an inescapable sense of disease in mixing the sensual with the spiritual, the will of the Divine has prevailed and determined that in the right context, with the right dose and manner – these contents pave the path towards a robust and libidally alive relationship with G-d. I humbly suggest that this tension was navigated by virtually all Orthodox commentary by sublimating and focusing their energies on developing the metaphor more than the poetry. Malbim, however, endorsed a different resolution. He simultaneously developed both aspects – both the body and the soul of the text. His work declares that the interpretation is only as meaningful as the poem is touching. It is only to the extent that our sensitivities and emotions are aroused by reading these humanly-rooted poems, that our imagination and spiritual-emotional repertoires become sensitized to extrapolating their messages to the realm of the Divine and metaphysical. Ultimately, Shir Hashirim—the Song of Songs—highlights the exceptional literary and psychological talents of the Biblical authors, and it demonstrates the breadth and variety of expression offered within the core of Judaism. The anomalous nature of this text amongst the Biblical canon underscores how the Torah is a "Tree of Life", that is, the Torah is all anchored in one trunk and one set of roots, but extends branches that produce myriads of diversely scented fruits and exquisitely delicate leaves. To pigeonhole this work, to me, is to lose the rich and integrative nature that sits at the core of the Jewish religious experience. Instead, we are called to engage with, appreciate, and grow through diverse religious texts and experiences, both intellectually and emotionally. Ultimately, Malbim provides the perfect bridge to do exactly that. My rendering of Shir HaShirim based on the Malbim offers the text to the reader as a beautiful, poetic, romantic drama that is coherent, textually beautiful, and emotionally meaningful. It is up to the reader to decide whether they engage with this as a springboard to soar into the metaphor – which I sincerely hope they do, or whether they prefer to remain anchored in the human and romantic elements – to fall for the body without its soul.
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Song 1
The country girl senses her former beloved standing outside the locked palace door. She speaks softly, as though to herself:
If only we weren't separated by the palace wall —
He could kiss me
With the passionate kisses of his mouth.
She turns toward the door and addresses him:
You realize,
Your love is dearer to me
Than the fine wines and luxuries
That surround me in the palace.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse:
Even the elite young women in this harem
Are in love with you,
Even though they have not seen you;
Because of the scent of your fragrant oils,
And your fine reputation that wafts like perfume oil.
One can only imagine how mesmerised they would be
Should they set their eyes on your beauty
And behold your virtue firsthand.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse:
Please draw me out of the palace —
My lady friends will come too;
We will all run after you!
I am confined here, brought by the king
To live with him in his chambers.
We will delight in the rush of freedom
And then permanently rejoice with you!
We will continuously recall your love —
More than the wine and royal luxury,
Because we genuinely admire who you are!
Palace luxuries offer fleeting self-indulgence;
You offer lasting virtue and substance.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse:
She turns to her attendants:
O' daughters of Jerusalem,
Tasked with watching my every step to ensure I do not escape:
Do not scorn me that I am dark skinned,
For in essence I am fair.
Just like the blackened tents of Kedar
In essence identical to the whitest sheeting of Shlomo —
They can regain their whiteness if thoroughly washed.
My darkness is but a deep suntan
From a life spent outdoors with my flocks;
Should I remain indoors, my fairness will return.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Do not surmise that you are beholding my true self
When you set eyes on my darkness,
For I was greatly exposed to the sun.
Besides my shepherding,
My mother’s sons tasked me with watching the vines,
Thus parching my flesh beneath the scorching sun.
I could not tend to my personal vine —
That is, my beautiful fair skin.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse:
She resumes her heart-to-heart with her beloved:
Tell me, love of my soul:
Where can I find you at pasture with the flocks?
Where can I find you resting in the afternoon shade,
Alongside the flocks of your fellow shepherds?
Although my every step is watched,
When I get the chance to escape I shall join you there!
For, how can I —
A free-spirited rural girl steeped in the outdoors —
Be enshrouded in the gloomy confines of this urban palace?
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse:
The shepherd boy responds:
O' fairest among the women,
That is impossible
Unless you know my location —
And this you can only find
By following in the footsteps of the sheep.
But you must also escape detection:
Throughout your journey to discover me,
Disguise yourself as a shepherd girl
And pasture your lambs near the shepherds' dwellings.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse:
The country girl heeds his advice, and one day — still bedecked in her royal jewellery — she escapes the palace and reunites with her beloved.
The shepherd boy, beholding her, says:
My one and only soul-mate —
It is as though my one and only horse was confiscated
To pull Pharaoh's chariot along with all his other horses.
Does not Shlomo have so many wives and concubines?
Yet he fancied you
And so deprived me of you,
My one and only love.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse:
That said — look at your breathtaking appearance!
How fair are your cheeks with their golden braids,
O' royal horse;
How grand is your neck with its strings of pearls.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse:
The silver droplets —
That you once owned as a simple country girl —
Have been transformed for you into golden braids!
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse:
The country girl replies:
The fine scent of you,
My spikenard-like beloved,
Reached all the way to the king's banquet.
I had no appetite —
My mind was preoccupied with you.
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse:
You, my beloved, are engraved on my heart;
I cannot stop thinking about you —
Like the scent of the sachet of myrrh
That rests between my breasts,
Its fragrance constantly arousing my senses.
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse:
You, my beloved, are like a vibrant cluster of henna
Whose fine scent wafts far and wide;
I smell you in Jerusalem
Although you are so distant,
In the vineyards of Ein Gedi.
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse:
The shepherd boy says:
You are so fair
Because you are my faithful soulmate.
Yes, you are so inherently fair —
Especially because your eyes are true to me,
Unfailingly faithful like a dove.
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse:
The country girl says:
You too are so physically attractive, my love,
Also so virtuous.
How I desire to lie with you here beneath the trees —
Look, the foliage that shall be our makeshift bed is lush.
text.0_Chapter, 16_Verse:
Let the forest cedars be the makeshift beams of our home;
The broad branches of the forest cypresses
The plumbery protecting us from rain.
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse:
I am like the Sharon tulip — beautiful and heliotropic,
And the lily of the valleys — whose delectable scent peaks at dusk.
In your shining company I unrestrainedly express my outward beauty;
In the shadowy palace I instead exhale my virtue of character.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Her lover responds:
Indeed, a tender but fragrant lily
Surrounded by thorns
Is the likeness of my soulmate
In the company of the court women.
My outnumbered but outstanding —
Distance yourself from them
Lest their barbs taint our pure love.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse:
The country girl replies:
My beloved too is like a fragrant and fruitful apple tree;
Though dwarfed by the towering forest trees,
He is the most attractive of them all.
I desire his shade and so there I shall sit;
How sweet are his fruits to my palate.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse:
She narrates:
He ushered me into the wine house
And spread his banner over me —
He showered me with love.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse:
I called out:
"Provide me with goblets of wine,
Lay out for me a bed of fragrant apples,
For I am lovesick."
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse:
He heeded my desire
And made love with me;
He placed his left hand under my head,
Embraced me with his right arm.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse:
But the court women of Jerusalem were hot on her trail.
She turns in their direction and exclaims:
I bind you under oath,
O daughters of Jerusalem —
Let the gazelles and does be witness:
Neither douse nor arouse our love!
Let me be;
Allow my desire to be realized.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse:
Song 2
With her escapade over, the country girl is returned to the palace, where she endures the long autumnal and winter months, far from her beloved. Then spring arrives, and with it her beloved shepherd boy, intent on reigniting their love.
The country girl speaks:
Behold! The voice of my beloved —
I detect it from afar!
He is coming now,
Leaping over the mountains,
Skipping over the hills,
Towards me.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse:
My beloved resembles a gazelle or a young hart
As he gracefully bounds across the landscape.
And here he is!
I sense him standing on the far side of our wall —
He observes me through the windows,
Straining to break through the lattice!
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse:
My beloved spoke up and said to me:Arise my beloved, o' my fair one —
The time is ripe to escape from here.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse:
For behold, the autumn has passed;
The winter rains are over,
Entirely gone.
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse:
The blossoms have appeared on the land,
The time for bird-song has arrived;
Even the chirp of the turtledove —
Returned from its winter migration —
Is heard in our land.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse:
The fig tree has produced its early green figs;
The grapevines their tender grapes
That give out their delectable fragrance.
Arise my soulmate, o' my fair one —
The time is ripe to escape from here.
The gloomy wintry past is behind us;
A bright and vibrant future awaits.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse:
My dove,
Nesting in the clefts of the rock,
Who dares not leave her confines
Nor sound her songful voice,
For she is in hiding,
Concealed in the precipice —
Show me your appearance,
Sound for me your voice,
For your voice is so pleasant
And your appearance so fair.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse:
One fine spring day, while strolling through the vineyards around Jerusalem, the country girl turns to her entourage:
"Go and seize for us the foxes —
Those pesky little foxes that damage vineyards —
For our vines are laden with tender grapes."
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse:
Having earned a few moments of privacy, she beckons to her beloved. He presents her with a bouquet of fine lilies, whereupon she contentedly exclaims:
My beloved is mine, and I am his —
He who pastures among the fragrant lilies.
text.1_Chapter, 16_Verse:
We can delight in each other's company
Until the peak of the day's heat
When the shadows shall flee
And my entourage returns from their foxhunt.
Then you must turn on your heels;
Make yourself once more
Like a gazelle or a young hart
On the towering fragrant mountains.
Just as they retrace their steps from time to time,
You too must come and visit me.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Song 3
The country girl, lying alone at night, recounts:
On my bed at night
I sought the man whom my soul loves;
I sought him but did not find him.
I was filled with an overwhelming longing
To reunite with him.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse:
I said to myself:
"Let me arise and roam the city square,
The market places,
The streets —
I will seek him whom my soul loves.
" I sought him but did not find him.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse:
My search drew me
To the outer environs of the city.
There I crossed paths with the sentries
Who circle the city's periphery.
I asked them:
Have you seen the man whom my soul loves?
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse:
When I found the man whom my soul loves.
I grabbed onto him —
This time I shall not let go of him.
I shall bring him to my mother's house,
To the room of she who conceived me —
To have him permanently nearby.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse:
But once again the court women of Jerusalem were hot on her trail.
She turns in their direction and exclaims:
I bind you under oath,
O daughters of Jerusalem —
Let the gazelles and does be witness:
Neither douse nor arouse our love!
Let me be;
Allow my desire to be realized.
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Once the country girl's repeat escapade became known to the court, there was much uproar, and an enquiry began:
Who is this ascending from the wilderness,
Enveloped in pillars of smoke-like fragrance?
Bedecked in fumes of incense —
Myrrh and frankincense,
All the powdery merchandise of the perfumer?
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse:
How did she escape the palace sleeping quarters?
Behold! The bedroom of Shlomo —
Sixty mighty warriors surround it,
Of the mightiest of Israel!
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse:
All of them sword-bearing,
All with combat experience!
Yet each one's sword was frozen by his loins —
Stricken with overwhelming fear
On those nights.
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse:
And how did she escape under the noses of her fellow courtiers?
King Shlomo had singled her out
For marriage as a premier wife!
King Shlomo had crafted a magnificent bridal canopy
For the country girl and himself —
He made it of Levanon wood.
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse:
Its pillars of silver,
Its beds of gold,
Its curtains of purple wool.
Its interior infused
With passionate flaming love —
More intense than the combined love felt towards
All the other court girls of Jerusalem.
text.2_Chapter, 10_Verse:
And while dwelling in the canopy in the lead-up to her wedding, she would encourage her upgraded entourage — now comprised of the elite "girls of Zion" — to feast their eyes on the ostentatious wedding preparations:
"Girls of Zion —
Go and take a look at the gorgeous crown
With which King Shlomo's mother crowned him
On his wedding day,
On the day his heart delighted."
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Once they were distracted, she would slink away to meet her beloved. And their love was most passionate. The shepherd boy, infatuated with her from head to toe, softly praises her:
Behold you are beautiful my soulmate —
You are so beautiful.
Your eyes shine forth as faithful as doves
From beneath your kerchief;
Your hair with its myriad shades —
Like a flock of goats
Descending from Mount Gilad.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Your teeth — so uniform, such a pristine white —
Like a flock of identical sheep
Just now ascended from their wash;
All harmonious,
No blemish among them.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse:
Your lips — a deep red —
Like a scarlet thread;
Your speech so fair.
Wrapped within your kerchief,
You are filled with inner beauty of character —
Like a slice of luscious pomegranate.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse:
Your neck is like the Tower of Dovid,
Built as a military fortress;
A thousand shields hang upon it,
With all the quivers of the mighty.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse:
Your two breasts — desirous twins —
Like two fawns
Pasturing among the fragrant lilies.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Let us delight in each other's company
Until the peak of the day's heat
When the shadows flee
And your entourage returns from its forages —
Then I must be off
To the mountain of myrrh
And the hill of frankincense.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse:
But how can I leave you
When everything about you is fair, my soulmate,
And you are without blemish!?
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse:
I shall arrange for you to come with me —
I shall take you as my bride;
With me you will come from the Levanon canopy.
You will look back at your captivity
From the peaks of Amanah, Snir and Chermon,
Where none shall dare pursue you
For fear of the lions' dens
And the mountains of leopards.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse:
You bound my heart to yours,
My equal — my sister.
You bound my heart to yours
With but one of your eyes,
With but a single pendant of your necklace.
Although one of your eyes is ever watchful,
On the look-out for those who pursue you,
And although I get to enjoy so little of you
Since King Shlomo has proclaimed you his —
You have still captivated my heart.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse:
How fair is your love, my sister and bride;
How your love surpasses wine for rousing my spirit,
And the fragrance of your perfumed oils —
All spices.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse:
The lovers draw close and passionately kiss. The shepherd boy remarks:
Your lips, my bride, are dripping with sweetness —
The honey and milk2[2] An ancient mouthwash formula.
Beneath your tongue;
The scent of your garments
Smelling like the royal Levanon canopy.
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse:
My sister and bride has saved herself for me;
She is to other men like a lush garden that is locked,
Its waters secured,
Its spring fastened.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse:
Your vegetation — delicious —
A pomegranate orchard with luscious fruits;
Fragrant with henna scents and spikenard scents —
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse:
Spikenard and saffron,
Calamus and cinnamon,
All the frankincense trees,
Myrrh and aloes —
All the major spices.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse:
The spring of your garden —
A well of life-giving waters
That flow forth from the royal Levanon canopy.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse:
The country girl responds:
Awaken, o' wind of the north!
Come, o' wind of the south!
Blow upon my garden —
Give off its fragrances!
Let my beloved come to his garden
And feast on its luscious fruit!
text.4_Chapter, 0_Verse:
The shepherd boy makes love and romantically sings:
I have come to my garden, my sister and bride!
I have gathered my myrrh with my spice,
Eaten my sugar cane with my honey,
Drunk my wine with my milk!
Now let us celebrate —
Let our friends eat,
Our loved ones drink
And become intoxicated!
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Song 4
But their love would not continue undisturbed. The country girl was tracked down once more and forcibly returned to the palace. Placed under permanent watch, the memory of her beloved gradually faded, and she slipped into court routine.
The country girl recounts:
I was sleeping soundly
Although my heart remained somewhat awake to my lover.
Then I heard the sound of my lover knocking at my door:
Open up for me,
My sister, my soulmate,
My faithful dove, my perfect one —
My head is saturated with dew,
My locks with the droplets of night.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse:
I replied:
I have already removed my robe for the night —
How can I put it back on?
I have already washed my feet —
How can I soil them once more?
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse:
But my beloved sent forth his hand from the portal
To try and unlock the door himself,
And my innards trembled for him
By my hitherto suppressed feelings towards him.
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse:
I arose to open the door for my beloved;
My hands coursed with passion —
As though dripping with myrrh,
My fingers imbibed with the scent of myrrh —
So long as they were hovering above the lock.
Yet each time I touched it,
The passion vanished into thin air
And I hesitated.
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Eventually I opened the door,
But my beloved had stolen away —
Stung by my ambivalence.
My life was knocked out of me
By his harsh departing words.
I searched for him but did not find him;
I called out to him but he did not answer.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse:
As my frantic search led me towards the countryside,
I crossed paths with the sentries
Who circle the city's periphery.
They hit me and injured me;
They stripped me of my adornments —
Those guards of the walls.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse:
Exasperated and defeated, she turns to her entourage:
I bind you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem:
If you find my beloved —
What shall you tell him?
That I am lovesick for him.
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse:
Surprised by the intensity of her love, her entourage asks:
How does your love differ from other loves,
O' fairest among women?
What makes your lover differ from other lovers —
That you have imposed this oath upon us?
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse:
The country girl responds, her voice now radiant:
The complexion of my beloved —
As fair as pure white,
As ruddy as red;
He stands out from the myriads.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse:
His head — as though
Plated with a sheet of exquisite gemstone;
His layered ringlets as black as a raven.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse:
His eyes gaze at me
Like a dove at a creek's torrent;
A pristine white as though bathed in milk,
Perfectly set in their sockets.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse:
His cheeks — chiselled
Like the furrows of a spice patch
In which perfumes are cultivated.
His lips like lily blossoms,
Dripping with wafting myrrh.
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse:
His arms — like golden cylinders
Filled with gems of Tarsus;
His stomach — as though
Plated with ivory sheets,
Translucent like sapphires.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse:
His legs — like marble pillars
Set in sockets of exquisite gemstone.
His appearance — as beautiful
As the royal Levanon canopy;
As strong as its cedars.
text.4_Chapter, 15_Verse:
His palate exudes sweet delights;
Everything about him is desirable.
This is my beloved,
This is my soul mate,
O daughters of Jerusalem.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Song 5
Deeply impressed by her descriptions, the entourage resolves to no longer harass the country girl; from now on they will help in her quest to reunite with him.
The entourage asks:
Where has your beloved gone,
O fairest among women?
In which direction did your beloved head?
We shall seek him with you.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Just then, the country girl looks up and sees her lover approaching from a distance.
She calls out:
My beloved has descended from the mountains,
Headed towards his garden —
Towards me, his prized spice patch.
He is coming to tend to the garden,
To gather his sweet-scented lilies — my love.
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse:
I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine —
He who tends to the lilies.
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse:
The shepherd boy arrives and beholds his beautiful bride once more:
You are so fair my soulmate,
Now that we have made up
And desire one another once more.
As splendid as all the girls of Jerusalem —
Now awesome and untouchable,
As though surrounded by military formations!
text.5_Chapter, 4_Verse:
Turn your eyes from my opponent —
From cautiously looking out for King Shlomo —
Gaze only at me,
For they make me proud.
Your hair with its myriad highlights —
Like a flock of goats
Descending from Mount Gilad.
text.5_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Your teeth — so uniform, such a pristine white —
Like a flock of identical sheep
Ascended from their wash;
All harmonious,
No blemish among them.
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse:
Like a slice of luscious pomegranate,
Filled with inner beauty of character,
Wrapped within your kerchief.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse:
He turns to her entourage and defiantly asks:
Are there not sixty queens,
Eighty concubines,
Countless young women at the king's service?
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse:
Yet he demands to possess my one faithful dove,
My one and only love!
Unique among her mother's offspring!
She who combines the choicest elements of beauty
For the woman who bore her!
All the girls who behold her approve of her;
All the queens and concubines praise her!
text.5_Chapter, 9_Verse:
The girls of the entourage approach the country girl:
Who is this who has come to gaze down,
Radiant like the breaking dawn?
Fair as the setting moon,
Clear as the rising sun,
Awesome as the star formations?
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse:
The country girl replies:
Consciously, I was simply descending to the garden of nuts,
To behold the vegetation lining the brooks —
To see whether the vines had blossomed,
Whether the pomegranates had bloomed.
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse:
I was not aware that subconsciously
The love of my soul had mobilized me like a chariot,
Transporting me from the palace
Back to my laypeople.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Realizing she is set on leaving the palace never to return, her entourage implores her to stay:
Do come back, O come back, counterpart of Shlomo!
Do come back, O come back —
We will look up to you.
But the country girl rejects them:
How can you look up to the counterpart of Shlomo
When she is a prisoner,
Encircled by two encampments?
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse:
Her entourage tries another approach:
How fair are your feet, O daughter of nobility,
So long as they rest in the fine shoes
Gifted to you by Shlomo —
Out in the country they will blister and crack.
That which your thighs conceal are like jewels
So long as they are fashioned by a craftsman.
Your extreme feminine beauty
Is contingent on maintenance and care
That only the palace can provide.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse:
Your navel — like a moonlit pool
Never lacking mixed wine;
Your stomach — like a heap of wheat
So long as you are hedged with lilies —
The luxury and bounty of the palace.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse:
Your two breasts — desirous twins,
Like two fawns;
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse:
Your neck — like an ivory tower;
Your eyes shimmer
Like the pools of Heshbon —
Worthy of a city gate frequented by the multitudes,
But wasted on villagers
Who cannot appreciate your beauty.
Your nose — perfectly straight,
Like the Tower of Lebanon
Overlooking the environs of Damascus.
text.6_Chapter, 5_Verse:
Your head sits atop your body
With a majesty akin to the Carmel crags;
Your hair sways around your head
Fine as royal purple —
The king has is love bound in its locks.
text.6_Chapter, 6_Verse:
Her entourage turns and philosophically addresses love:
How fair and pleasant you are, O love —
When complimented by sensual delights.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse:
Now King Shlomo himself appears and attempts to win back the heart of his beautiful fiancée:
This posture of yours is like a palm tree —
So magnificent and tall;
Your breasts hang so high
Like its date clusters.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse:
I said to myself:
I must climb this palm tree —
Its trunk is tall and smooth
But I shall clutch its bark protrusions.
I beg you —
Should I successfully climb to your heart —
May your breasts be to me
Like the clusters of the vine;
The scent of your breath
Wafts from your nose like fragrant apples —
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse:
Your palate like delightful fine wine…
But the country girl defiantly cuts him off:
No — it shall go to my beloved,
To he who embodies honesty,
To he who makes my sleeping lips murmur:
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse:
I am my beloved's,
And his desire is upon me.
text.6_Chapter, 11_Verse:
She turns to her lover:
Come, my beloved —
Let us head out to the fields,
Spend the night in the villages
Surrounding Jerusalem.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse:
Let us rise early for the vineyards;
See if the vine has blossomed,
If the tender grapes have emerged,
If the pomegranates are in bloom.
Regardless of their condition —
My love for you has ripened;
There I shall give you my love.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse:
The mandrakes yield their fragrance for everyone;
Outside our doors grow all delectable fruits.
They may be fresh but feel old —
Dulled by abundance and habituation.
But my love for you is fresh and untainted;
I have hidden it solely for you.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse:
Thus the country girl and her beloved leave the palace for good, and head off for life together in the fields. But while deeply in love with the shepherd, she begins to pine for the creature comforts of her former palace life. She shares her fantasy with her beloved:
If only you could have been an equal to me —
As though you were my brother,
Nursed by my mother's breasts.
If only you had been a member of the royal family,
Receiving the same 'maternal' care I did —
Then I could kiss you
When encountering you out in the open,
And no one would scorn me.
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse:
I could lead you,
Bring you into my 'maternal' home —
You could teach me.
I could offer you spiced wine
And my pomegranate nectar.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse:
She snaps back to the passionate love of her present reality, and airs her thoughts as though addressing her former entourage:
But now he unabashedly makes love with me;
He places his left hand under my head,
Embraces me with his right arm.3[3] Here I partially departed from Malbim due to contextual clues; particularly the reference to her lover in third person implying a new audience, and the juxtaposition of 2:6–7 that would parallel the juxtaposition of 3–4.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse:
Need I bind you under oath,
Daughters of Jerusalem!?
How could you douse or arouse our love,
Interfere with my desire being actualized!?
You no longer have any power over me.
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse:
The narrator questions:
Who is this palace maiden
Who rises from the wilderness
Yet holds her beloved so close?
The shepherd boy responds:
No — in her essence,
She is a fellow countrywoman.
Beneath the apple tree I first aroused you;
There your mother's womb contracted with you;
There she who bore you
Caused her own mother's womb to contract.
text.7_Chapter, 5_Verse:
The country girl turns once more to her lover:
Set me like a seal upon your heart,
A seal upon your arm —
May you always cherish me
And protect me from the desirous king.
For although our love is as intense as death,
The king's jealousy is as harsh as the grave.
But ultimately our love shall triumph —
Its blaze is ablaze
With roaring flames.
text.7_Chapter, 6_Verse:
The narrator reflects:
Indeed, love shall ultimately triumph.
Many waters cannot douse love;
Raging rivers cannot sweep it away.
Even if a man — as wealthy as Shlomo —
Offers all the wealth of his estate
To rupture the lovers' bond,
They will simply scoff at him.
text.7_Chapter, 7_Verse:
Song 6
The country girl turns to her lover, concern upon her face:
We have a little sister —
A fellow country girl;
She is still young and has no breasts.
What can we do for our sister
On the day she is discussed in the royal court?
How can we spare her my ordeal
; Save her from the clutches of the king?
text.7_Chapter, 8_Verse:
The shepherd boy answers pragmatically:
If she is as resolute as a wall
In her adamance to evade the king,
We can build about her a fortress of love —
Find her a suitor who will enrapture her.
But if there are gaps in her defences,
As though she is a door —
Sometimes open to cooperation with the king —
We must board her up with panels of cedar.
text.7_Chapter, 9_Verse:
The little country girl chimes in:
I am like a wall;
My breasts — as unconquerable as turrets.
Therefore, in his eyes, I am viewed as one
With whom it is worthwhile
To seek a begrudging peace.
He knows I am indefatigable;
He has resigned himself to never possessing me.
text.7_Chapter, 10_Verse:
Shlomo has already tried me once —
He had a vineyard in the plain of multitudes,
In which he cultivated endless vines.
He entrusted this vineyard to caretakers;
Each presented him with one thousand pieces of silver
For its vast fruit yield.
text.7_Chapter, 11_Verse:
This became my vineyard,
Which Shlomo placed entirely at my disposal.
But I rejected it:
The thousand silvers are yours, Shlomo —
As well as the two-hundred share
For those who took care of its fruit.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse:
The shepherd boy glances anxiously around him, deciding he had better take his leave:
Listen — you who sit
In the rural suburbs of the city:
Fellow people are listening in to our conversation.
I must return to the safety of the wilderness —
But do let me hear your voice
From time to time.
text.7_Chapter, 13_Verse:
She replies:
Flee, beloved one —
Make yourself once more
Like a gazelle or a young hart
On the fragrant spice mountains.
Just as they retrace their steps from time to time —
You too please come and visit me.
